source.title: How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization?
source.authors: Shibani Santurkar; Dimitris Tsipras; Andrew Ilyas; A. Ma̧dry

record.tranche_reason: Compares VGG training with and without BatchNorm and reports training performance; this tests the BatchNorm part of V6.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results for noisy BatchNorm and alternative normalizations. Those findings are included only where they measure the training behavior V6 names. Loss-landscape and internal-covariate-shift measurements do not measure V6's accuracy claim.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares training accuracy over steps for VGG on CIFAR-10 with and without BatchNorm, including different learning rates. This is an original source for V6, so no verdict labels are assigned.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute BatchNorm's optimization benefits to a smoother loss landscape and more predictive gradients, rather than distributional stability. They also report similar benefits from other normalization schemes.
record.recipe_differences: Tests BatchNorm's training-performance effect on VGG/CIFAR-10. The text does not state a random-initialization comparison or an explicit replication of the original BatchNorm study's recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Training comparison is reported on VGG/CIFAR-10; the reported test accuracy differs with data augmentation. The training-speed plots compare learning rates 0.1 and 0.5, but numerical tolerance boundaries are not reported.

fits_no_version.finding: BatchNorm improves final test accuracy from 80% to 83%, and from 88% to 92% with augmentation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BatchNorm improves VGG generalization accuracy on CIFAR-10 under these recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: BatchNorm improves training loss in 25-layer deep linear networks on synthetic Gaussian regression.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BatchNorm accelerates optimization in deep linear regression networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Alternative activation normalizations yield training performance comparable to BatchNorm; L1 normalization performs better in deep linear networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Several activation normalization schemes can improve optimization without BatchNorm's variance normalization.

record.problems: Training-accuracy and learning-rate comparisons are figure-only, without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The text does not give a numerical learning-rate tolerance boundary.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows omitted. Loss-landscape, gradient-predictiveness, and internal-covariate-shift measurements were left out because they do not measure the accuracy behavior named in V6.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error across network sizes, CIFAR-100, and corrupted or random labels is not established by the supplied results.
Teacher-student ReLU networks, spurious-minimum frequencies, and extra student neurons.
Depth comparisons, identity shortcuts, and the specified alternatives for training very deep networks.
Comparisons of activation-matched initializations, signal propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth. Using Glorot initialization alone does not test these effects.
Initial linearized stability limits, catapult recovery, curvature trajectories, and edge-of-stability training.
Sigmoid networks on MNIST, Inception on ImageNet, and normalization-free residual training with Fixup. Learning-rate robustness is examined, but no numerical tolerance boundary is reported.

missing.what: The VGG training-accuracy comparison at learning rate 0.5 is omitted from R1. Figure 1 and its caption report a consistent BatchNorm training-speed advantage across the displayed learning rates; exact curve values cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

The training-accuracy panels at learning rate 0.01 provide an additional VGG comparison with and without BatchNorm. Record these separately from the ICS measurements; the caption reports better accuracy with BatchNorm.
Under the same activation noise used for noisy BatchNorm, the unnormalized network fails to train, whereas noisy BatchNorm retains its training advantage. This control is absent from the rows.

record.verdict_notes: This study is explicitly an original source for V6; its results receive no supports, limits_scope, or challenges labels. Figure 10 measures local gradient predictiveness across hypothetical step sizes, not independent training runs establishing learning-rate tolerance. The record also incorrectly suggests initialization is unstated: Appendix A.1 specifies standard Glorot initialization for both architectures.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests VGG training speed with BatchNorm on CIFAR-10. It does not report a numerical learning-rate tolerance boundary. It does not test Fixup or residual networks.

rows.subject: VGG (Standard + BatchNorm)
rows.operation_detail: Train VGG with BatchNorm and compare training accuracy against standard VGG.
rows.note: The text describes a consistent gain in training speed with BatchNorm; the plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: The reported training-speed gain is supported by the Figure 1 caption and Section 2. Figure 1 also includes learning rate 0.5, which this row does not capture.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 1(a) and caption; Section 2; Appendix A.1, pp. 2–3, 12.

rows.subject: VGG (Standard + BatchNorm)
rows.operation_detail: Train VGG with BatchNorm; report test accuracy and compare with standard VGG.
rows.note: The paper gives these test accuracies while describing the VGG architecture.
rows.check: The 83% versus 80% test accuracies are correctly transcribed, but endpoint generalization accuracy does not establish faster training or greater learning-rate tolerance.

rows.subject: VGG (Standard + BatchNorm)
rows.operation_detail: Train VGG with BatchNorm; report test accuracy and compare with standard VGG.
rows.note: The paper reports the augmented-data results parenthetically.
rows.check: The augmented-data test accuracies, 92% versus 88%, are correct, but do not measure training speed or learning-rate tolerance.

rows.subject: VGG (Standard + “Noisy” BatchNorm)
rows.operation_detail: Train VGG with time-varying non-zero-mean, non-unit-variance noise added to batch-normalized activations.
rows.value: Nearly matches standard BatchNorm; figure only
rows.note: The text says noisy BatchNorm nearly matches standard BatchNorm training performance and both outperform the standard network.
rows.check: Section 2.1 explicitly reports that noisy BatchNorm nearly matches ordinary BatchNorm and both train better than the unnormalized network. The small difference from ordinary BatchNorm does not make the gain over the unnormalized baseline partial.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

rows.locator_found: Figure 1(a) and caption; Section 2; Appendix A.1, pp. 2–3, 12.

relation.reason: Controlled comparisons directly test BatchNorm's effect on training speed and learning-rate tolerance.

tranche.reason: This is an original V6 source, directly measuring the stated effect through training-accuracy trajectories for VGG/CIFAR-10 with and without BatchNorm.

source_check.notes: Appendix A.1 explicitly specifies standard Glorot initialization, contrary to the recipe note's assertion that initialization is unstated. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate; training-speed gains are stated qualitatively without numerical speed estimates.
